opinions.rationale: Restricting analysis to records with observed eligibility can cause selection bias, but systematic differences between included and excluded patients do not alone establish bias for a specified causal estimand. Identification depends on conditional exchangeability for the observation or selection process and adequate observed support. When true eligibility is missing not at random, the effect among truly eligible patients is generally not identified from the main data alone. However, assessing the criterion for everyone in a validation source is sufficient, not necessary. A probability validation subsample, auxiliary-variable restrictions, explicit parametric assumptions, sensitivity analysis, or partial-identification methods can also inform the problem. If eligibility is a deterministic threshold of an underlying measurement, imputing that measurement and deriving eligibility can target the same population as directly imputing eligibility. Changing imputed membership across draws represents missing-data uncertainty and does not automatically change the estimand. Existing weighting work addresses an important identified-assumption case, while the unrestricted latent-eligibility problem remains open.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Complete-case eligibility restriction can bias an emulation when observation of the criterion depends on treatment or outcome determinants not adequately controlled in the recorded history. If true eligibility among unobserved records is missing not at random, the effect in the truly eligible population requires additional identifying assumptions or external information. Validation data are one useful source of such information, and imputing the underlying measurement versus the eligibility indicator requires different models even though coherent implementations can target the same causal estimand.

resolving_work.title: Adjusting for selection bias due to missing eligibility criteria in emulated target trials
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Provides a weighting approach for selection arising from missing eligibility information under identifying assumptions; it does not nonparametrically identify unrestricted missing-not-at-random latent eligibility.

opinions.rationale: Conditioning on an eligibility variable opens a noncausal path only when that variable is a collider, or a relevant descendant of one, in the assumed causal structure. Being a healthcare-use variable is not sufficient. The stated treatment-to-eligibility-to-outcome timing is also imprecise: eligibility fixed before time-zero treatment cannot be caused by that subsequent treatment or its subsequent outcome. The relevant graph may instead involve prebaseline treatment decisions, incipient disease, or common causes of treatment and outcome. Causal discovery does not universally return only a Markov equivalence class; what can be oriented depends on temporal, interventional, functional-form, and latent-confounding assumptions. It nevertheless cannot certify collider status from unrestricted observational data. An advisory tool for identifying possible temporal or collider problems remains an open development problem, but the asserted medium-high severity is context dependent rather than general.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Conditioning on a baseline healthcare-use eligibility variable can induce selection bias when, in the assumed causal graph, it is a collider or a relevant descendant of a collider involving determinants of treatment and outcome. Temporal checks and causal-discovery methods under explicit assumptions can flag possible problems, but observational data alone cannot generally certify the required causal structure, so domain-grounded causal review remains necessary.
